job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Jade Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My alarm goes at 6:40. I take the 7:52 bus from Mill Road, where I share a flat with two others, to Pryce & Hale, a small accounting firm in Ashby. I'm a junior on the audit side, so I tick invoices against bank statements and chase clients for missing receipts. It's dull, but I like the moment a set of books finally balances. By evening I'm tired, I cook pasta, and I check my student loan balance more often than I should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected. At work I'd tell Dilnaz, the senior who sits next to me, that the software saves a few minutes and that's all. Online I'd say the hype was mostly a way to sell subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel relieved but not calm. My job is safe enough, but I'm on 23,500 a year and my loan payment plus rent leaves me about 90 a month. Nothing changing means that stays exactly as it is, and it isn't enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd ask for a pay review after my first year, join the accountants' union branch a colleague mentioned, and start the chartered exams if the firm pays the fees. I'd put 40 a month into savings even though it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It feels like running on a treadmill, steady but never getting anywhere. I'm not scared of AI in that world, I'm scared of my overdraft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the union. What would you say to your boss if he asked why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mr. Pryce straight that a junior on 23,500 with 41,000 of debt needs someone in the room with her. He's decent, so he'd nod and then probably change nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if something breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract, then the gym I barely use. Never the rent, because Tess and Kofi, my flatmates, would be stuck. I'd ask the loan company for a pause, which they only give for a few months.

say: Good, that's what I expected. The software saves a few **minutes** and nothing more.
I'd tell Dilnaz (my senior) the hype was mostly a way to sell **subscriptions**.
think: I feel relieved but not calm, because after rent and loan I keep about **90 a month**.
Nothing changing means my thin pay and **debt of 41,000** stay exactly the same.
do: Ask for a **pay review** after my first year at Pryce & Hale.
Join the accountants' **union** branch a colleague mentioned.
Put **40 a month** into savings and start the chartered exams if the firm pays.
feel: Tired, like a **treadmill** that never gets anywhere, and scared of the overdraft more than of AI.
S0.quote: My job is safe enough, but I'm on 23,500 a year and my loan payment plus rent leaves me about 90 a month.
fieldNote: Safe job, but money is the whole story; **debt** drives her more than AI does.
Plans to join a **union** from the start, in line with her left-leaning views.
Keeps the familiar path and avoids new tools; she wants a **pay review**, not a new skill.

steps.text: Keep ticking invoices at Pryce & Hale and ask for a pay review
Join the accountants' union branch a colleague mentioned
Move 40 a month into a savings account on payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the juniors who pay for this. Firms like ours will stop hiring people to tick and match, and they'll call that efficiency. I'd say it loudly to Dilnaz and on the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is exactly what gets eaten. Ticking invoices against statements is the first thing software does. I might still be here in two years, but nobody will be hired behind me, and then I'm the cheapest person to let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union branch and ask what the firm owes juniors if tasks move to software. I'd keep my head down at work, do the checking by hand and be very accurate, because that's my edge. I'd save every spare pound and look at a council finance job, since public bodies move slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, and a bit sick. I did the degree, I took the loan, and now the entry rung is being sawn off. I don't blame the software, I blame the owners who'll keep the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the checking by hand. Wouldn't the software be faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would, yes, and I know that's the contradiction. But I don't trust it, and I've never used these tools, and Mr. Pryce signs off my work, not a machine. If the firm tells me to use it, I'll learn it slowly and grudgingly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dilnaz. She's got a daughter at nursery and she's the one the firm would cut if they decided one senior was enough. If it came to a choice, I think they'd keep the person who costs less, and that's me.

say: The **juniors** will pay for this, and firms will call it efficiency.
I'd say it loudly to Dilnaz and on the **union** group chat.
think: My job is exactly what software eats first, so nobody will be **hired** behind me.
If cuts come, I'm the **cheapest** person to let go.
do: Ask the union branch what the firm **owes** juniors if tasks move to software.
Check by hand and be very **accurate**, since that's my edge.
Save every spare pound and look at **council** finance jobs.
feel: **Angry** and a bit sick, because the entry rung is being sawn off after the loan.
S1.quote: I did the degree, I took the loan, and now the entry rung is being sawn off.
fieldNote: Blames **owners** who keep the savings, not the software itself.
Admits the contradiction of checking by hand, then says she would learn AI **grudgingly** if told to.
Worried for a **colleague** with a child as well as for herself.

steps.text: Ask the union branch what the firm owes juniors if tasks move to software
Keep checking invoices by hand and aim for zero errors
Apply for junior finance jobs at the local council
Save every spare pound into a three-month buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I'd say that's a disaster and nobody in charge is ready. I'd say governments must protect people with real support, not leaflets about retraining. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd say it to my MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished in accounting. Anything on a screen with numbers is the first thing it does better and cheaper. I've got a loan of 41,000 and under a month of savings, so there's no time and no cushion. Robots in 2031 hardly matter to me, because my work goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to my MP and turn up to every union action. I'd try to get any extra shifts, maybe evenings at the supermarket on Station Road, so I can build a few months of rent. I'd ask my loan company in writing what happens if I lose my income. I honestly don't know what else I could do, because I've no savings to retrain on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It's the feeling when the lift drops. I'd lie awake counting how many weeks of rent I could cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mum I'm fine, because she cleans offices at 5 a.m. and she's got her own worries. Then I'd cry in the bathroom. She sacrificed for this degree, and I'd feel I've wasted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the firm let you go, what happens first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose the room on Mill Road within two months and probably move back to Mum's sofa, forty minutes away, and sign on for support. I'd be 23 and starting again with debt.

say: This is a **disaster** and nobody in charge is ready.
Governments must give real **support**, not leaflets about retraining.
think: I think I'm **finished** in accounting, because screen work with numbers goes first.
With 41,000 of debt and under a month saved there's no **cushion** to retrain on.
do: Write to my **MP** and go to every union action.
Take extra **evening** shifts to build a few months of rent.
Ask my loan company in **writing** what happens if I lose income.
feel: **Frightened**, like a lift dropping, counting weeks of rent at night.
Ashamed that the degree my mum sacrificed for might be **wasted**.
S2.quote: I'd lose the room on Mill Road within two months and probably move back to Mum's sofa, forty minutes away, and sign on for support.
fieldNote: Sees **no time** and no cushion; the two-year clock makes retraining feel impossible.
Protects her **mum** from worry and cries privately, which shows the gap between say and think.
Turns fear into **politics**: MP, union, public support.

steps.text: Write to my MP about support for young graduates
Attend every union action and the next branch meeting
Take evening shifts at the supermarket for extra rent money
Ask the loan company in writing about payment pauses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a little room but not much. I'd say it to Tess and Kofi over dinner. The government has to start now, with unions at the table, or it'll be too late again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be anxious the whole time but not frozen. In five years I could clear a good part of the loan if I keep my job, and I could be a senior by 26. Then the thinking jobs go anyway. So I'd be running against the clock to get out of debt before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the loan by 100 a month by moving into a cheaper room, and use the union to push the firm for a training promise. I'd study for the tax exam, because tax advice for ordinary people might need a human a little longer. And I'd stay close to Mum, who might need me if things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but with a thread of hope. There's a path where I'm out of debt by 2031 and the world is different but I'm not drowning. That keeps me going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still study for the exam if you thought the work might vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because I don't know that it will vanish, and the exam might open a job that isn't just ticking. It's a gamble, and I hate gambling, but standing still is a gamble too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at work in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing visible. The partners will bring in software on the quiet, and we'll hear after. I'd want the union to have asked beforehand, in writing, that no junior loses a job because of it.

say: Five years is a little room but **not much**, and unions must be at the table.
I'd tell Tess and Kofi (my flatmates) the government must **start now**.
think: I'd be anxious the whole time but not **frozen**, since there's time to get out of debt.
The real race is clearing the **loan** before the thinking jobs go anyway.
do: Overpay the loan by **100 a month** by moving to a cheaper room.
Press the **union** for a written training promise from the firm.
Study for the **tax** exam, since ordinary people may need a human adviser longer.
feel: Heavy, but with a thread of **hope** that I'm out of debt by 2031.
S3.quote: There's a path where I'm out of debt by 2031 and the world is different but I'm not drowning.
fieldNote: Five years turns fear into a **race**: clear the debt first.
Dislikes gambling yet accepts the **exam** as the less risky gamble.

steps.text: Overpay the student loan by 100 a month
Move to a cheaper room in the Mill Road area
Study for the tax exam in evenings and weekends
Push the union for a written no-job-loss promise on software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say it's the first time anyone's given us enough room. I'd say to the union and to politicians that this is the moment to build proper support, shorter weeks, retraining that pays you while you do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more settled. By 2036 I'll be 32, the loan could be nearly gone and I might have a different career or even a family plan. It's still scary, but a decade is a life, not a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the accountancy job and pay down the debt first, no rush to change. In about three years I'd start moving to something that works with people, like advice for tenants and households on money. I'd keep up with the union and vote for anyone serious about public support. And I'd try learning the tools slowly, since I'd have time to get comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others. There's a kind of respect in being given time, and I'd use it well. I'd still have a knot in my stomach about Mum's pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the tools slowly. What changes your mind about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. If I'm not being rushed, I can try one thing at a time without feeling I'm helping them replace me. I'd probably start with something like a spreadsheet helper, and see if it's actually useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in place by then, from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guaranteed income floor, free retraining with pay, and rules that make firms share the savings. I don't want handouts for their own sake, but I want a fair share of what the machines make.

say: Ten years is the first time anyone's given us enough **room**.
This is the moment to build proper **support**, like paid retraining.
think: By 2036 I'll be 32, the loan could be nearly gone and I might have a **family** plan.
A decade is a life, not a **countdown**, though I still worry about Mum's pension.
do: Keep the accountancy job and pay down the **debt** first.
Around year three, move towards **money advice** for tenants and households.
Try one AI **tool** at a time, starting with a spreadsheet helper.
feel: Calmer than in the other pictures; being given **time** feels like respect.
S4.quote: A decade is a life, not a countdown.
fieldNote: The only picture where she feels she can **choose**, and she moves towards people-facing work.
Her resistance to AI **softens** when she isn't rushed.
Wants a fair **share** of machine savings, not handouts.

steps.text: Pay down the loan before changing careers
Train in money advice for tenants and households from year three
Try one AI spreadsheet helper at work for a month
Vote for parties that back an income floor and paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's the only picture where I've got no way out. I've got debt and no savings, and no time. What would help is real support that arrives fast: a guaranteed income, loan payments paused, and rent help, not a course I can't afford to attend.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people like me aren't lazy or stupid. We did everything we were told, and we still ended up with the risky bit. I'd like someone to remember that when they decide what to do.

headlineQuote: We did everything we were told, and we still ended up with the risky bit.
portrait: **Jade** is 22, an accounting graduate in her first junior audit job in Ashby, renting a shared room on **Mill Road**.
She carries **41,000** of student debt, saves almost nothing and has no family money to lean on.
She prefers the familiar, has never used AI tools and trusts **unions** and public support more than employers.
Her fear rises sharply with speed: uneasy at slow change, **alarmed** at the two-year picture.
Ten years of warning would let her clear debt and move into **money advice** work.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because she has debt, no savings and no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Fast **support**: a guaranteed income, paused loan payments and rent help, not a course she can't afford.
People remembering that her generation did what it was told and still took the **risk**.
